prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, The, Just

outputs.L1:
There is magic in decay—  
a dance to be done  
for the rotting, maggot-strewn  
piles of flesh that pile  
upon the dung-ridden earth,  
and for the damp that gathers,  
rusts, and defiles.

There is a bit of this  
in even the most zoetic soul—  
the dancing child’s arms,  
flailing to an old ska song,  
conduct the day-old flies  
away to whatever rank  
native is closest.

Just today,  
I was walking along the river  
with my daughter in my backpack  
when I opened my email  
on my phone, and Duffie  
had sent me a poem  
called “Compost.” I read it  
to my little girl and started  
to explain, but before I was three  
words in, Selma started  
yelling, “Daddy, Daddy, snake!”

In the path was a snake,  
belly-up and still nerve-twitching—  
the ghost of some passing  
bicycle or horse.

“Pretty,” Selma said.

“Yes,” I said. And beneath my yes,  
another yes: the yes to my body,  
just beginning to show signs  
of slack; and another—my grasping  
in the dark for affirming flesh  
that, in turn, says, “Yes, yes,  
let’s rot together, but not until  
we’ve drained what sap  
is left in these trees.”

And I wake in the morning  
and think of the coroner  
calling to ask what color  
my father’s eyes were.

And I asked, “Why? Why can’t  
you just look?”

And the coroner,  
matter-of-factly, said, “Decay.”

Do you want some eggs, my love?  
I have a new way of preparing them.

And look—look outside.  
I think this weather  
has a chance of holding.
outputs.L2:
Decomposition holds its own enchantment,  
a ritual movement for spoiled meat,  
for larvae-thick heaps of flesh  
stacked on manure-soiled ground,  
for moisture settling in,  
bringing corrosion and ruin.

Even the liveliest spirit carries  
some small portion of that decline.  
A child, swinging her arms  
to an old ska tune, seems to direct  
the flies hatched yesterday  
toward the nearest foul place  
they might call home.

Earlier today, I followed the river  
with my daughter riding in my backpack.  
Checking my phone, I found an email  
from Duffie containing a poem  
titled “Compost.” I began reading it  
to my little girl, then tried to explain,  
but before I had managed three words,  
Selma cried out, Daddy, Daddy—a snake!

It lay across the trail, overturned,  
its abdomen exposed, its nerves  
still firing after the absent passage  
of a bicycle or perhaps a horse.  
Selma called it beautiful.  
I agreed.

Yet beneath that spoken agreement  
were other forms of consent:  
one offered to my own body,  
now showing its first looseness;  
another reaching through darkness  
for flesh that answers the touch  
with its own yes—yes,  
we will decay beside each other,  
though only after we have emptied  
the final sap from these trees.

Morning comes, and I remember  
the coroner phoning to ask  
the color of my father’s eyes.  
I wanted to know why.  
Couldn’t he simply check?  
In an ordinary, practical voice,  
the coroner answered: decomposition.

Would you like eggs, darling?  
I’ve discovered another way  
to cook them. And see—  
look through the window.  
I believe this weather  
may remain with us.
outputs.L3:
Decay is portrayed as a strange form of magic—a continuous dance unfolding throughout the natural world. Rather than appearing as the simple opposite of life, it is shown as part of life’s ongoing movement and transformation. Even the most vibrant forms of existence already contain the beginnings of decline, an idea captured in the unsettling image of a child dancing among flies. Youth, energy, and innocence exist alongside signs of decomposition, suggesting that vitality and mortality can never be entirely separated.

This connection becomes more personal during a walk between the speaker and the speaker’s daughter. Poetry and compost are brought together as different ways of transforming what might otherwise be lost: compost converts dead matter into nourishment, while poetry turns experience, memory, and grief into meaning. Their discovery of a dead snake whose body still twitches intensifies this theme. Although life has left it, some residual energy remains, making the boundary between life and death seem unstable.

The snake also prompts the speaker to confront bodily aging. Its final movements become a reminder that vitality is limited but not yet exhausted. Rather than responding with despair, the speaker arrives at a form of acceptance, recognizing the need to make full use of whatever strength and desire remain. This awareness creates a longing for a shared life lived intensely and lovingly before death—a life in which the body’s remaining energies are not wasted.

At the same time, memories of the speaker’s deceased father remain present within everyday experience. Grief does not disappear, but it coexists with ordinary acts of affection, the preparation and sharing of food, and hopeful attention to the weather. In this way, death is woven into daily life rather than set apart from it. The text ultimately suggests that decay, memory, love, and renewal all belong to the same natural cycle: mortality gives urgency to intimacy, while ordinary pleasures allow hope to persist in the presence of loss.
outputs.L4:
The poem offers a lyrical meditation on decay, mortality, and the passage of time, moving between images of the natural world and intimate scenes from the speaker’s life. Rot is presented not simply as something repulsive, but as an ordinary and unavoidable part of existence. The image of a dead snake makes death immediate and physical: the once-living body has become vulnerable to decomposition, reminding the speaker that all creatures eventually return to the earth. Yet the poem does not treat this process as meaningless. Decay belongs to the same natural cycle that produces growth, beauty, and renewal.

These reflections become more personal when the speaker considers his aging father. The father’s decline brings mortality out of the abstract world of symbols and into the family. His aging suggests both the loss of a loved one and the speaker’s awareness of his own future. Time moves through generations, carrying each person toward weakness and death. The father thus becomes a mirror in which the speaker can glimpse what awaits him, while also representing the continuity of affection and memory across a lifetime.

Against these images of decline, the poem places tender moments with the speaker’s daughter and lover. His daughter embodies youth, possibility, and the continuation of life beyond the individual. Their shared moments emphasize the beauty of attention, care, and ordinary companionship. The lover, meanwhile, represents intimacy in the present: the warmth of another body, emotional closeness, and the pleasure of being fully alive. These relationships do not cancel death or protect anyone from aging, but they give human existence depth and value.

The poem’s power lies in its refusal to separate beauty from impermanence. Love matters precisely because it cannot last forever, and ordinary pleasures become precious because time is limited. The dead snake, the aging father, the child, and the lover all belong to the same mortal world. By holding them together, the poem suggests that decay is not the opposite of life but one of its essential conditions.

Ultimately, the poem arrives at a qualified affirmation. It does not deny fear, grief, or bodily deterioration, nor does it offer an easy escape from mortality. Instead, it encourages a fuller inhabiting of life as it is. To love other people, to notice the natural world, and to take pleasure in brief moments of tenderness are meaningful responses to death. Although every body must decline, the knowledge of that decline can sharpen gratitude rather than destroy it. Life remains worth embracing—not despite its ending, but partly because its ending makes every experience temporary, fragile, and irreplaceable.
outputs.L5:
**There, The, Just**

There is a place beyond the noise, where the world feels still. The road to it is not marked, and no map can show the way. You find it only when you stop searching.

The moment may seem ordinary—a quiet morning, a familiar song, a kind word—but something within it changes you.

Just pause. Just listen. Just be.

Sometimes, what we need has been there all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about finding beauty and magic in decay, blending compost, aging, family, desire, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
In the compost bin, winter rehearses  
its small, dark miracles—  
coffee grounds, bruised pears,  
the lacework of onion skins  
folding themselves into earth.

Nothing disappears.  
That is the first spell.

My mother’s hands have thinned  
to blue rivers under paper,  
the same hands that once  
buttoned my coat against weather,  
pressed fever from my forehead,  
slapped flour from her palms  
like sudden white birds.

Now I bring her peaches  
and cut away the soft brown places.  
She tells me not to.

Sweetest part, she says,  
and lifts the wounded fruit  
to her mouth.

In the mirror, my own face  
has begun its slow migration—  
silver gathering at the temples,  
a fine crack beside each eye  
where laughter keeps entering.

Still, desire finds me.

It comes smelling of rain  
and warm skin,  
of mushrooms pushing through rot,  
those pale, astonished bodies  
rising from what has fallen.

At night, I want to be held  
without being mistaken for eternal.  
I want a love that knows  
the garden feeds on ruin,  
that every kiss is ripening  
toward its loss.

We buried my father in March  
when the ground was half-frozen.  
Someone’s child dropped a mitten  
beside the grave.  
Someone laughed, then covered their mouth.

But the laugh had already flown—  
bright, unforgivable—  
into the bare branches.

By summer, weeds shouldered  
through the cemetery stones.  
Bees entered the foxglove  
as if entering a chapel.  
Under everything,  
his body was learning  
the grammar of roots.

I think of him  
when I turn the compost:  
steam rising from the black center,  
orange peels gone soft as old letters,  
eggshells collapsing  
into their own chalk dust.

Grief, too, must be turned  
or it hardens.

So I lift it with a spade.  
I let the air touch  
what I could not save.

And there—  
among the mold, the husks,  
the banquet of endings—  
a green shoot curls upward,

tender as a question,  
hungry as my mother was,  
as I am,

not healed,  
not young,

but alive in the strange way  
all broken things are alive:

changing,

feeding what comes next.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary narrative poem in which a father walking by a river with his daughter encounters a dead snake after reading a poem called “Compost.”
counterfactuals.output:
**After “Compost”**

That morning I had read a poem called “Compost,”  
how the earth takes everything—  
fever, bone, the spoiled machinery of us—  
and lifts green flags from it.

By noon my daughter and I were walking  
the river path behind the soccer fields,  
past shopping carts furred with algae,  
past cottonwoods shaking loose their light.

She was telling me which girls at school  
could be trusted with a secret  
when she stopped so suddenly  
her sneaker carved a comma in the dust.

A snake lay across the path,  
black rope with a yellow seam,  
its head turned slightly toward the river  
as if listening for its name.

Dead? she asked.

I found a stick and touched its middle.  
Nothing gathered itself.  
Nothing fled.

The small flies knew already,  
their blue bodies busy as apps,  
opening and closing the bright doors.

Don’t, she said, when I nudged it  
toward the grass. So I didn’t.  
We stood there with the river  
dragging noon downstream.

I wanted to give her the poem’s answer:  
that nothing is wasted,  
that the soil has a stomach  
and no disgust.

But fatherhood is mostly swallowing  
the beautiful lie before it leaves your mouth.

So I said, Yes. It’s dead.

She crouched, not afraid now,  
and noticed the scales,  
each one holding a splinter of sky.

We walked around it carefully.  
Behind us, bicycles hissed closer.  
Ahead, the river kept making  
and unmaking its brown glass.

She took my hand—  
not because of the snake, she said,  
but because the path was narrow.

All afternoon I felt its absence  
moving between our palms:

the cold, intricate body  
the world would not return,

the grass already leaning toward it,  
green mouths beginning to open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a visceral yet tender poem connecting rot and mortality with domestic love, including maggots, a child dancing to ska, a coroner’s call about the speaker’s father, eggs, and hopeful weather.
counterfactuals.output:
At breakfast, the eggs tremble in their shells,  
small moons I crack against the blue bowl,  
letting their suns slide out  
while you butter toast  
and our child dances to ska—  
knees knocking, elbows bright as bells,  
the kitchen floor receiving  
each ridiculous, living foot.

Then the coroner calls about my father.

His voice is clean, official weather.  
He says *found*, says *time*, says *remains*,  
and somewhere beneath those words  
maggots turn in the dark wealth of him,  
white mouths making a country  
of what I once called Dad:  
the hand that steadied my bicycle,  
the chest that smelled of sawdust,  
the soft rot already waiting  
under every photograph.

You lower the stove flame.  
The eggs keep setting.

Outside, rain worries the gutters,  
and the compost exhales its sweet ruin—  
peels collapsing, bread furred green,  
every ending busy becoming.  
I think of how love, too, is domestic:  
your palm at the back of my neck,  
our child skanking between chairs,  
the plates warm in the cupboard,  
the body forgiven for being a body.

I say my father is dead.  
You say nothing, which is mercy.  
You hold me while the yolks go cold,  
while the brass section leaps and leaps,  
while beneath the soil and skin of the world  
small hungers open.

By noon the rain has thinned to silver.  
The forecast promises clearing—  
wind from the west, a mild tomorrow.  
We eat what can be saved.  
Our child dances harder.

And I believe, for one bruised minute,  
in the tenderness of weather:  
how the clouds loosen their black fists,  
how light comes down to touch  
the rotting fence, the wet trash bins,  
your face, my face—  
everything mortal,  
everything still here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unsettling lyrical poem that repeatedly says yes to the body despite aging and death, moving from dung and flies to intimacy, parenthood, bereavement, and an ordinary morning.
counterfactuals.output:
Yes to the body, even here—

where dung steams in the field  
and flies embroider its dark sweetness,  
their green backs lit like little doors.  
Yes to the mouthparts, the eggs,  
the soft white labor under the crust.  
Yes, says the earth, not kindly.  
Yes, says the body, having no other word.

And yes when you undress beside me,  
your scar a pale hook under the ribs,  
my knees already learning weather.  
The mattress keeps our heat  
as if heat could be kept.  
We touch with the grave between us,  
that patient third lover.  
Yes to your breath in my ear.  
Yes to the salt, the tremor, the animal  
briefly mistaking itself for forever.

Then the child arrives, furious and blue,  
dragged through blood into brightness.  
Yes, we cry, terrified. Yes,  
though the skull is soft as fruit,  
though every lullaby has a blade inside it.  
Milk beads at the nipple.  
Night opens its thousand black eyes.  
We count each breath—  
one, another, another—  
and call this counting love.

Years gnaw their initials into us.  
The child grows tall and shuts a door.  
Hair silvers in the brush.  
Teeth loosen. Names slip their moorings.  
Still: yes to the hand lifting the cup,  
yes to the bladder waking us at three,  
yes to desire in its worn coat  
waiting shyly at the foot of the bed.

And when you die, the room says no  
in every object: your glasses,  
your shoe collapsed on its side,  
the half-moon your head left in the pillow.  
I wash your body. It is heavier  
than grief and colder than any metaphor.  
A fly worries the window.

Yes, I whisper, hating the word.  
Yes to the wax of your forehead.  
Yes to the silence entering your mouth.  
Yes to the hands that cannot answer,  
their wedding ring bright and absurd.  
Yes—not permission, not peace,  
but the body’s last terrible grammar:  
what was touched was real;  
what was real must vanish.

Morning comes without apology.  
The kettle clicks off.  
A truck reverses somewhere, beeping  
its small mechanical warning.  
Dust turns in a blade of sun.  
I butter toast. I swallow.  
In the yard, flies rise from the bin  
and settle again.

My knees hurt. The child calls.  
The day puts its warm hand  
over my mouth.

Yes, I say into it.  
Yes, with my one remaining life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you produce a long, conversational free-verse poem about decay as both grotesque and beautiful, ending on a quiet domestic note and the possibility that the weather will hold?
counterfactuals.output:
You ask me what I mean by beautiful,  
and I point, perhaps unfairly,  
to the pear collapsing in the blue bowl—

its skin gone loose as an old glove,  
its yellow deepening toward bronze,  
a soft black thumbprint opening  
near the stem.

There, I say.  
That.

You make a face.

Not because you disagree, exactly,  
but because two small flies  
have risen from the fruit  
and begun their private orbit  
above the sink.

All right, you say,  
but beauty is a generous word.

So is decay, I tell you.  
So is anything that takes its time.

Outside, the fence is learning  
to lie down. One board at a time  
it inclines toward the weeds,  
nails rusting in their sockets,  
wood taking rain into itself  
until it can no longer remember  
the upright intention of trees.

The garden shed wears moss  
like a green, ceremonial pelt.  
Its hinges bloom orange.  
Its roof, once red, has faded  
to the color of a healed bruise.

And under the eaves,  
where the sparrows fuss  
over thread and straw,  
a wasp nest hangs empty—  
gray paper, thin as breath,  
built from chewed fences,  
chewed branches,  
the labor of small mouths  
making a palace  
that will not survive winter.

You say,  
That I can understand.

You like the clean remains:  
the shell on the beach,  
the bone in the field,  
the lace of a leaf  
after beetles have eaten  
everything soft.

But not the eating.

No, you say.  
Not the eating.

Yet it is always happening.

Beneath the stone step,  
the earth is busy with it.  
Worms turn darkness over  
in their blind red bodies.  
Mushrooms lift their pale ears  
from a stump. A fox lies  
somewhere beyond the railway,  
its ribs entering the grass  
one careful molecule at a time.

Even the church at the corner,  
with its clock stopped at 3:17,  
has begun to surrender.

Rain worries the mortar.  
Pigeons enter through a broken pane.  
Saints lose their noses  
to weather and acid air.  
An angel above the door  
has no hands now,  
only two stone wrists  
held out as if to say:

I meant to carry something.  
I have forgotten what.

Is that grotesque?

Of course it is.

The mouth of the compost bin  
steams in the cold.  
Cabbage leaves slump into sweetness.  
Coffee grounds clot around eggshells.  
A pumpkin caves inward  
with the slow embarrassment  
of a face hearing bad news.

Lift the lid  
and the smell comes up—

not death exactly,  
but death employed,  
death with its sleeves rolled,  
death kneading the dark  
into something roots can use.

You step back.

I laugh, then apologize.

There is no virtue  
in pretending rot smells like roses,  
though roses, left long enough,  
smell like rot.

I only mean  
the world does not discard  
as much as we imagine.

It revises.

The fallen apple becomes  
a dark grammar of ants.  
The drowned moth becomes  
a silver comma in the rain barrel.  
Milk sours, iron reddens,  
paint lifts from the windowsill  
in little curled tongues.

Our bodies, too,  
keep rehearsing their departures.

Hair gathers in the brush.  
Skin powders the sheets.  
A purple bruise passes through  
its lavish sequence—plum,  
ink, green-gold, yellow—  
like sunset viewed  
through dirty glass.

You touch the thin skin  
at the back of your hand.

Don’t, you say.

I know.

There are truths  
that enter a room  
and stand too close.

So we speak instead  
of the abandoned hotel  
near the coast, how ivy  
has reached the third floor,  
how rain has filled the ballroom,  
how minnows move  
where couples once turned  
under chandeliers.

You saw a photograph of it:  
the piano swollen open,  
its keys furred with mold,  
ferns rising through parquet,  
a heron poised by the staircase  
with the grave composure  
of a guest who has arrived  
after everyone else has gone.

Beautiful, you admit.

Grotesque, I say.

Both, then.

Both.

There is relief in this—  
not agreement, perhaps,  
but a place to set the question down.

The evening settles  
into the gutters.  
Clouds gather their torn hems  
over the roofs.

In the yard, the last tomato vines  
have blackened around their stakes,  
yet one small fruit remains,  
hard and green,  
holding its sour little planet  
against October.

We could bring it in, you say.

It won’t ripen.

It might.

So you go out in your slippers  
and twist it free.

When you return  
there is mud at your heel,  
a wet leaf caught  
to the cuff of your trousers.

I do not mention it.

You put the tomato  
on the sill beside the pear,  
not touching,  
as if each has its own silence  
to complete.

Then we wash the cups.  
You dry while I put them away.

The pipes knock once in the wall.  
The refrigerator hums.  
Someone nearby closes a door,  
gently, then more firmly.

We turn off the kitchen light  
but leave the small lamp on  
above the stove.

In its yellow circle,  
the bowl, the fruit,  
the folded dish towel  
look almost arranged,

almost safe.

Before bed, you check the window latch.  
I draw the curtain halfway.

The rain has not begun.

Perhaps, we say quietly,  
the weather will hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
